common_name: Zephirine Drouhin Rose (Thornless Fragrant Climbing Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring against a fence, arbor, or wall; Zephirine Drouhin is one of the few climbing roses with no thorns, making it a good choice for planting near walkways, and it tolerates partial shade better than most roses.

directions: Plant against a sturdy support in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Introduced in France in 1868, Zephirine Drouhin is a Bourbon climbing rose beloved for two rare qualities in one plant: it is almost completely thornless, making it pleasant to train and prune, and it is intensely, classically rose-scented, with large, cerise-pink, semi-double flowers produced in repeated flushes through the growing season rather than once. It tolerates more shade than most roses, which makes it useful on a partly shaded fence or arbor where sun-hungry modern roses would struggle. It is more susceptible to black spot in humid climates than newer disease-resistant roses, so good air circulation and occasional fungicide treatment in wet years help keep the foliage healthy.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring; the climbing form of Cecile Brunner is extremely vigorous and needs a large, sturdy support, while the original bush form stays much smaller and suits a mixed border.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Introduced in 1881 and universally known as the Sweetheart Rose, Cecile Brunner produces small, perfectly formed, high-centered buds in soft pale pink that open to dainty, lightly fragrant blooms, traditionally favored for boutonnieres and small posies because of their miniature, exquisite shape. It exists in both a compact bush form suited to a border and a famously vigorous climbing sport that can scramble thirty feet or more into a tree if left unchecked, so gardeners should choose the form that fits their space. It is a tough, easy rose with good disease resistance and needs only routine pruning to control its size, particularly for the climbing form.

common_name: Green Velvet Boxwood (Cold-Hardy Rounded Hybrid Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Velvet is a hybrid between English and Korean boxwood bred for good winter color retention and a naturally tidy, rounded form that needs little shearing.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade with some afternoon shade in the hottest part of zone 9. Bred in Canada as a cross between English and Korean boxwood, Green Velvet combines the fine, dense texture prized in English boxwood with much better cold hardiness and improved resistance to winter bronzing, holding a rich, consistent dark green color through the year better than many older cultivars. Its naturally tidy, rounded habit needs only light shearing to maintain a formal shape, making it a popular low-hedge and edging plant. Like other boxwoods it requires sharp drainage to avoid root rot and benefits from monitoring for boxwood leafminer, the main pest of concern in Southern gardens.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese boxwood tolerates heat and humidity better than English boxwood, making it a common low-hedge choice across the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Japanese boxwood is a heat- and humidity-tolerant relative of Korean boxwood long used across the Southern United States for clipped hedges, foundation plantings, and parterre-style formal gardens, valued for its small, glossy, rounded leaves and dense, easily shaped growth. It handles the long, hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season better than English boxwood, which often struggles in southern zones, though it still requires sharp drainage since all boxwoods are prone to root rot in soggy soil. Shear one to two times a year to maintain a formal shape, or leave it looser and prune selectively for a more natural look, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the main pest to monitor in Southern plantings.

common_name: Autumn Embers Encore Azalea (Deep Red Reblooming Compact Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Autumn Embers is a compact, deep red-flowered selection from the reblooming Encore azalea series, flowering in spring and again in summer and fall.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with protection from harsh afternoon sun in the hottest part of zone 9. Autumn Embers is a compact-growing selection within the Encore reblooming azalea series, producing deep, rich red double flowers in the main spring flush and then again through summer and fall, giving significantly more color over the season than traditional once-blooming azaleas of similar size. Its smaller mature size compared to many Encore cultivars fits foundation plantings and smaller borders where a full-sized azalea would outgrow the space. Water deeply during dry spells, especially before the later bloom flushes, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom to avoid removing the buds destined for later color.
